===== CONTEXT.md =====
# Test Case Validation

An API server that checks TestLink test cases field by field and writes accepted
ones through to TestLink via `testlink-mcp`. Callers are AI agents, so a rejection
is expected to be read, corrected, and retried rather than reported to a human.

## Language

### Subject

**Test Case**:
The unit submitted for validation, composed of named fields. Always the whole
case, never a fragment — a caller submits a case, not a field.
_Avoid_: test, test script, TC, case

**Field**:
One named part of a test case or a reference document, carrying its own rule
set. Fields are validated independently; a violation in one does not exempt the
others from checking. The fields of the two never overlap, and neither do their
rule sets: a rule written for one cannot reach the other.
_Avoid_: attribute, property, key, column

**Reference Document**:
Material the generating agent reads to write test cases from, served over the
API because the agent has no local files at all. Composed of named fields the
way a test case is — a title and a body — so the rules reach it and a read
reports what fired. Read only: a document the agent could write is one it could
author in the style the rules exist to catch and then read back as authority.
Carries no rejection, because nothing is ever submitted.
_Avoid_: reference, doc, guide, corpus, source material

**Test Suite**:
The container a Test Case lives in, and the unit a caller places a submission
into. Suites nest: a suite may sit under another suite of the same project.
Carries no rule set — rules bind to the fields of a test case, so a suite is
served through unchecked.
_Avoid_: folder, group, category, collection

**Project**:
The outermost container TestLink holds, owning its suites. Named by a caller
alongside the suite, never fixed at deployment: TestLink is the store the
caller works in, so where a case belongs is the caller's to say. Carries a
prefix, stamped into the external id of every test case it holds and fixed at
creation; deleting a project takes everything under it, so the prefix is what a
caller restates to confirm the delete.
_Avoid_: workspace, product, repository, area

### Rules

**Rule**:
One check applied to one field, either satisfied or violated. A rule names what
it looks for and the reason it gives when it fires.
_Avoid_: check, constraint, assertion, validator

**Rule Set**:
The rules bound to a single field. Every field has its own; there is no global
rule set applying across fields. Not a thing written down anywhere — each rule
names the field and the content it belongs to, and a rule set is the enabled ones
that name a given field. So a rule is added or switched off on its own, and no
rule can reach a field it was not written for.
_Avoid_: profile, policy, ruleset, config

**Rule Set Version**:
What names the rules a response was produced by, carried on every response. Derived
from the rules in force rather than declared beside them, so it cannot go on naming
rules that have since been changed. It covers everything a caller was judged by —
the field, the rule id, the kind of check, what is looked for, the flanking, the
reason and the exceptions — and leaves out disabled rules, which judge nothing. The
id is in there though nothing looks for it in a field, because it is what a
violation carries: two rule sets a caller reads differently are not one. The same rules
always produce the same version, so a rule switched off and later switched back on
returns the version to what it was rather than to a new one meaning the same thing.
Fixed for the life of a running server, because rules are read once at startup and
never reloaded.
_Avoid_: revision, build, tag, release, hash

**Term**:
A word or phrase a rule looks for in a field — either vocabulary that must be
used or wording that must not appear. Matched whole and in any casing: a term is
written once rather than once per capitalisation it turns up in, and it does not
fire inside a longer word, where a word runs on through a hyphen or an
underscore. The words of a phrase are matched however they are spaced, a line
break included.
_Avoid_: keyword, word, phrase, vocabulary, jargon

**Symbol**:
A single character a rule looks for in a field. Distinct from Term: a Term is
matched as a word, a Symbol as a character.
_Avoid_: special character, punctuation, glyph, sign

**Flanking**:
A condition on a symbol rule that fires it only where whitespace surrounds the
character, so the same character stays legal inside a word without needing an
Exception. The edge of a field counts as whitespace, so a character opening or
closing a field is flanked. Distinct from Exception: Flanking narrows where a
rule looks, an Exception suppresses it where it would otherwise fire.
_Avoid_: word boundary, padding, delimiter, spaced

**Exception**:
A word or phrase attached to a rule that suppresses it where the rule's match
falls inside it, leaving the rest of the field under the rule. Written the way a
Term is and found the same way — in any casing, however its words are spaced —
but found wherever it turns up, inside a longer word included.
An Exception belongs to exactly one rule — there is no shared exception list.
_Avoid_: allowlist, whitelist, ignore list, false positive, override

### Outcomes

**Violation**:
One rule firing on one field, carrying the reason returned to the caller. The
unit of everything the API reports; a response is a list of violations.
_Avoid_: error, issue, finding, warning, failure, defect

**Rejection**:
The API's refusal to write a test case through to TestLink because it produced
at least one violation. Rejection is the only failure mode — there is no partial
or provisional write.
_Avoid_: block, reject state, quarantine, fail

########## 0001-validation-is-outside-the-agent-trust-boundary.md
# Validation is outside the agent's trust boundary

The agent that generates test cases cannot reliably validate them at scenario
level, so validation is split into a separate service the generating agent
reaches only over HTTP. Rules are baked into the deployed image rather than read
from a mounted path, and there is no rule-reload endpoint — the agent has no
mechanism by which it could relax a rule that keeps rejecting it.

## Consequences

Rule changes require a rebuild and redeploy performed outside the generation
workflow. This is deliberate friction: a rule set the generating side can edit
is not a boundary.
########## 0002-detection-is-deterministic.md
# Detection is deterministic; the model never decides a violation

Every violation is produced by literal term or symbol matching, not by a language
model. A local model is used offline to survey the corpus and surface candidate
rules a human then writes; once written, that rule is deterministic forever and
the model has no further part in it.

## Considered Options

Running fields through a local model in the request path was the obvious reading
of "validation with Ollama" and was rejected. The API sits in a write path and
returns rejections an agent must act on, which requires verdicts that are
identical across runs and explainable to the person whose test case was refused.
A 9B model gives neither.

## Consequences

The model's role shrinks over time rather than growing — each rule promoted from
survey to rule set is one less thing needing inference. Detection classes that
cannot be expressed as literal matching (duplication, ambiguity, unstated
preconditions) are out of scope until a deterministic expression is found.

########## 0003-agent-works-only-over-the-api.md
# The generating agent works only over the API, never local files

The agent that creates test cases reads existing cases and reference documents
through this API, not from markdown or any other file on disk. It has no local
working copy of the corpus.

## Considered Options

Letting the agent keep local markdown was the obvious approach and was rejected.
Agents corrupt structured markdown reliably enough that skills and rules do not
prevent it, and a local copy is also a second source of truth that drifts from
TestLink. Serving everything over the API keeps one source of truth and leaves
the agent with no file it can quietly rewrite.

## Consequences

Reference documents must be reachable through the API, so document serving is in
scope for this project even though it is not validation. The read path becomes
the only channel by which the agent sees existing content, which makes it the
place where legacy fingerprints would otherwise propagate into new cases.
########## 0004-rule-sets-live-in-a-database.md
# Rule sets live in a database, read once at startup

Rule sets move out of YAML files and into a database. Only the store changes:
they are still read once when the server starts and never reloaded, so a running
server judges every test case by the rule sets it started with.

The database is not scoped to rule sets, and this ADR does not fix its scope.
The maintainer's framing is that it is where strictly validated content lands,
and that it may later become the source of truth imported into production
TestLink, or a cache in front of it. Those are open. What is settled here is that
rule sets are among the things it holds.

## Considered Options

**Files, kept in version control.** Argued for on the grounds that version
control already gives history, review before a rule can reject anything,
one-command rollback, and a rule set version derived from the text as supplied.
Rejected by the maintainer. The store this project already reaches for is a
server rather than a working copy — TestLink replaced the local test case
markdown files for the same reason — and the file argument answers for one rule
set at a time, where the pressure comes from many of them copied and tweaked from
each other.

## Consequences

**ADR-0001 no longer describes the store accurately.** It says rules are "baked
into the deployed image rather than read from a mounted path". Neither half will
be true. The property that ADR-0001 exists to protect survives unchanged: rule
sets are read once at startup, there is no reload endpoint, and the generating
agent reaches the server only over HTTP, so it still has no mechanism by which it
could relax a rule that keeps rejecting it. The README already flags this tension
as open pending deployment shape; that flag now resolves to a database.

**Rule Set Version is unaffected.** It stays derived from the rule sets as
supplied and fixed for the life of a running server, because reading once at
startup is exactly what is being kept.

**The server stops being stateless.** The README records "no storage layer... a
database waits until a real requirement for one appears". That wait is over, and
a component the project has so far done without now has to be run, backed up, and
reachable from the server at startup.
########## 0005-reference-documents-are-checked-content-in-the-database.md
# Reference documents are checked content, held in the database

> Partly superseded by ADR-0006. The "How content reaches the database" section
> below, and the consequence "There is one write path, and the server is not on
> it", are no longer how this works: there is no load command, and an operator
> writes with SQL. Everything else here still holds. The text is left as it was
> written, because what it records is the decision as it was taken.

Reference documents live in the database ADR-0004 introduced, and they are the
first thing to make that database real. They are composed of named fields the
way a test case is — a title and a body — each with its own rule set, so a read
carries the violations found in what it serves. They are read only: the API
lists them and retrieves one, and there is no endpoint that writes one.

This settles the question the README carried as open, "what the reference-document
endpoints look like", and it fixes one part of the scope ADR-0004 deliberately
left open.

## Considered Options

**Where the documents live.** A directory on the server, pointed at by an
environment variable the way rule sets were, was argued for on the grounds that
it ships immediately, needs no new infrastructure, and keeps the boundary that
matters — the agent has no local files, and the server having them is exactly
the trust boundary. Storing them in TestLink as requirement specifications was
argued for as keeping one source of truth. Both were rejected by the maintainer
in favour of building the ADR-0004 database now and making documents its first
tenant: the store was already decided, and a second temporary store would have
been a third place content lives.

**Whether a read reports violations.** Serving documents straight through,
unchecked, was argued for as the smaller change and the one that invents no
vocabulary: a rule set was defined as the rules bound to one field of a test
case, and a document had no fields. Rejected by the maintainer. ADR-0003's own
reasoning applies to documents at least as strongly as to test cases — the read
path is where legacy fingerprints propagate into new cases, and a reference
document written in the wording the rules exist to catch is the most direct way
for that to happen. Documents therefore gained fields so the rules could reach
them.

**Whether the agent can write a document.** Full CRUD, matching the test case
surface, was considered and rejected. A document the agent could write is a
document it could author in the style the rules catch and then read back as
authority, which is the same reason ADR-0001 gives it no way to reload a rule.

**How content reaches the database.** Seeding on first startup was rejected
because it makes the server something that writes its own rules, and because
"first startup" is a state that is easy to get wrong on a redeploy. Loading
entirely out of band was rejected because it would leave no supported path from
a written rule set to a running server. A load command the operator runs was
chosen.

## Consequences

**Rule sets gained a level.** A rule set is now written under the content it
checks — `testCase:` or `referenceDocument:` — because the two have different
fields and a flat namespace would leave `title` belonging to nothing in
particular. Existing rule set files must be re-indented under `testCase:`. The
loader refuses a rule set naming anything else, so a file that was not migrated
fails loudly rather than binding to nothing and never firing.

**The server no longer reads a file.** Rule sets are read from the database at
startup, which resolves the tension the README flagged against ADR-0001: there
is no mounted path any more. Reading once at startup and never reloading is
unchanged, and so is rule set version, which is still derived from the rule set
text exactly as supplied.

**There is one write path, and the server is not on it.** `npm run load` is the
only thing in the project that writes to the database. The object the server
holds exposes no write at all, so relaxing a rule or authoring a document is not
something the running system can do, whatever reaches it over HTTP.

**Rule sets are appended, not replaced.** Superseding a rule set does not destroy
the one a running server is still judging by, so an operator can read back,
compare or recover what was in force before a load. Nothing in the API resolves a
version to its row — reading one back is an operator with a database client, not
a feature — so this is history kept cheaply, not a lookup the server offers.

**A document's shape is taken from its file.** The file name without its
extension is the id a caller retrieves it by; the first line is the title,
written as a Markdown heading; the rest is the body. Every file in the directory
is read as a document — a file that is not one is refused by name rather than
skipped, because a document silently left out is one the agent will never know it
was meant to have. Names opening with a dot are the exception, being the
operating system's rather than the operator's.

**One report covers everything an operator supplied.** The load command checks
the rule sets and the documents before writing either, and reports their problems
together. A rule set problem must not hide a document problem, or the operator
loads twice to find both — the same bargain the server makes at startup when it
names every invalid rule at once.
########## 0006-rule-sets-and-documents-are-written-with-sql.md
# Rule Sets and Reference Documents are written with SQL, and the project ships no loader

An operator writes Rule Sets and Reference Documents into the database with SQL,
using whatever database client they already have. The project ships the schema
and stops there: there is no load command, nothing read off the filesystem, and
no template to copy. The server reads the database at startup exactly as before.

This reverses the "How content reaches the database" section of ADR-0005, which
chose a load command the operator runs. Everything else that ADR settled is
untouched — documents are still checked content held in the database, still
read-only over the API, still composed of a title and a body with their own Rule
Sets.

## Considered Options

**A load command reading files.** What ADR-0005 chose and what this replaces. Its
templates and its directory of documents were the thing that made the database
concrete while the schema was being designed; the maintainer's framing is that
they were a development intermediate whose job ended when the database became
real, and that keeping them means the project carries two representations of the
same Rule Sets for the rest of its life.

**A write surface on the server, kept off the agent's API.** Rejected. It is the
most usable answer for an operator without a database client, but it puts a write
path on the process ADR-0001 exists to keep off one, and defends the property by
network reachability rather than by the server holding an object that cannot
write. The weaker guarantee was not worth the convenience.

**Writing with SQL, out of band.** Chosen by the maintainer. ADR-0005 rejected
this on the grounds that it leaves no supported path from a written Rule Set to a
running server. That objection is answered rather than dismissed: the schema
ships in the repository as `schema.sql`, the README documents the statements that
write a Rule Set and a Reference Document, and the suite extracts and runs those
statements against an in-process Postgres, so what is documented is what is
tested. The path is supported; it is simply not automated.

ADR-0005's other objection, to seeding on first startup, is not answered because
it no longer applies: nothing seeds. The server gained no write, and "first
startup" is not a state anything here behaves differently in.

## Consequences

**The project no longer writes to its own database, at all.** ADR-0005 recorded
"there is one write path, and the server is not on it". There is now no write
path in the project. What ADR-0001 protects is stronger for it, not weaker: the
agent cannot relax a Rule that keeps rejecting it, and neither can anything this
repository ships.

**YAML stays, as the storage format.** Rule Sets are held as text in
`rule_sets.source` and parsed at startup, which is what the load command already
wrote and what the server already read. Removing the loader does not remove
YAML — an operator writes YAML inside a SQL statement — so the Rule Set
vocabulary, its checking, and the Rule Set Version derived from the text as
supplied are all unchanged.

**A Reference Document's shape is no longer taken from a file.** Its id, and its
two Fields, were read out of a file name and a Markdown heading; an operator now
writes all three directly. The Rules that reach a document are unchanged, and so
is what a read reports. What goes is the file convention and the refusal of a
file that is not a document.

**Applying the schema becomes an operator's step.** The load command created the
tables on first use. A fresh database now has none until `schema.sql` is applied,
so the server's refusal to start has to name that step rather than a command that
no longer exists. A database with no schema is still told apart from a database
that is unreachable, exactly as before.

**Nothing checks what an operator wrote before the server binds it.** The load
command validated Rule Sets and documents together and reported every problem in
one pass. Startup still refuses invalid Rule Sets and still reports every problem
at once, so that check survives — it happens when the server starts rather than
when the Rule Set is written. A malformed Reference Document is no longer refused
at all: its Fields are whatever the operator wrote.
########## 0007-a-rule-is-a-row-and-is-disabled-rather-than-deleted.md
# A Rule is a row, and is disabled rather than deleted

Rule Sets stop being one YAML document held as text and become rows, one per
Rule. A Rule carries the content and the Field it binds to, which kind of check
it is, what it looks for, the reason it gives, and a switch. An operator adds one
Rule, or turns one off, with a single statement naming that Rule alone.

Nothing is deleted. A Rule that should stop firing is disabled, and its row
stays. What a Rule looks for is not edited either — the reason it gives is. Both
are a discipline the schema documents and does not enforce, which is a decision
rather than an omission: there is one operator, and a guard's value is entirely
in who it stops.

This changes only how Rule Sets are stored and edited. They are still read once
at startup and never reloaded (ADR-0004), still written by an operator with SQL
with nothing in the project writing (ADR-0006), and a Rule still binds to exactly
one Field of one kind of content.

## Considered Options

**One YAML document, appended.** What this replaces. Its virtue is that the Rule
Set Version falls straight out of the bytes, and that a superseded document stays
readable because a new one is inserted beside it rather than over it. Its cost is
that every edit is an edit to the whole thing: turning off one Rule means
retyping every other Rule into a fresh `insert`, and a Rule Set of sixty Rules is
a wall of text where a one-character slip in an unrelated Rule is invisible. The
maintainer's framing is that a Rule Set is a list of independent checks and
should be edited as one.

**Rows, deleted when no longer wanted.** The obvious shape, and rejected. Every
response names the Rule Set Version and every Violation is logged against it, so
the system has already promised to explain a rejection after the fact. A deleted
Rule breaks that promise silently: the log still names the Rule, and the Rule is
not there to be read. The test cases rejected by it stay rejected and become
unexplainable, which lands on the QA engineer who wrote them rather than on the
operator who deleted the Rule. Delete also buys very little — a disabled Rule
stops firing exactly as completely as a deleted one, so what is saved is table
size, at a scale (tens of rows) no database notices.

**Rows, disabled rather than deleted.** Chosen. `enabled` is both the switch and
the tombstone, so the operator has three operations rather than four and the
record of what once fired survives. Turning a Rule back on is one statement and
restores the exact Rule that was there, rather than a retyped approximation of
it.

**A table per kind — one for Terms, one for Symbols.** Considered because the
columns differ: a Symbol carries Flanking and a Term does not. Rejected. A
Field's Rule Set is one list that mixes both, so two tables means every read is a
union and every operation an operator performs has to start by working out which
table the Rule is in. One table with a column naming the kind keeps the statement
shapes identical.

## Consequences

**The Rule Set Version is derived from the Rules in force, not from text.** It
was a hash of the YAML exactly as supplied; there is no longer a document to
hash. It becomes a hash over the enabled Rules, rendered in a fixed order and
including everything a caller was judged by — the Field, the kind, what is looked
for, the Flanking, the reason, and the Exceptions. Disabled Rules are left out,
because they judge nothing.

What the version is for is unchanged: it names the Rules a response was produced
by, and it cannot go on naming Rules that have since been edited. One property
improves. Because the version comes from the Rules rather than from their
formatting, the same Rules always produce the same version — so a Rule disabled
and later enabled again returns the Rule Set to the version it had before, rather
than to a new one that means the same thing. Under the old scheme, reformatting
the YAML changed the version without changing a Rule; that no longer happens, and
the safety argument for it no longer applies, because there is no formatting left
to change.

**What a Rule looks for cannot be edited; what it says can.** Changing `looks_for`
or the kind of check makes it a different check under the same name, and every
Violation already logged against that name then describes something that never
happened. Changing the reason changes only the wording the caller is handed.
Rewording a reason changes the Rule Set Version, which is correct: what a caller
is told is part of what the Rules do.

An operator who wants a Rule to look for something else disables it and adds
another, which is the honest shape of that change anyway.

**The discipline is not enforced, and that is decided rather than left open.**
Everywhere else, this project has made the unwanted thing impossible rather than
forbidden — the server holds an object with no write (ADR-0006), the agent has no
reload endpoint (ADR-0004). This is the exception, and it is worth naming as one.

The enforcing move exists: a trigger refusing a `delete` on `rules`, and refusing
an update that touches the identity columns, naming what to do instead. Postgres
takes it. What it cannot do is live in `schema.sql`, because the suite runs the
shipped schema against pg-mem, and pg-mem cannot parse
`create function ... language plpgsql` — adding the trigger makes the schema
unrunnable there and fails thirteen tests. So enforcing it means either giving
the suite a real Postgres, or shipping the trigger in a second file the suite
does not run.

**Chosen by the maintainer: neither. The discipline stays a discipline**, written
in the schema's comments and in this ADR, with nothing stopping a `delete`.

The reason is the whole of it: **there is one operator, and it is the maintainer.**
A guard's value is entirely in who it stops. It stops the person who does not know
the rule, or who has forgotten it — and here there is no such person. Paying for a
wall against yourself, today, is paying for nothing. The other two options were
priced at roughly thirty-five lines and one afternoon, and at a test suite that
must start a real database; neither is expensive, and both buy the same nothing
while the operator count is one.

An API in front of the database was raised and rejected on the merits, twice over.
It would give this project the write path ADR-0001 and ADR-0006 exist to remove,
and it would not even work: the operator writes SQL directly, so they are already
past any door an API could guard.

**What makes this reversible, and what the trigger would be.** The day a second
person writes SQL against this database, the calculation changes and this should
be revisited. The upgrade is small and does not disturb anything here: a
`schema-guards.sql` carrying the trigger, applied once, plus a startup check
asking whether the guard is installed and refusing to start when it is not. That
check is a read, so the server gains no write and ADR-0006 is untouched. It is
recorded here so the option does not have to be rediscovered.

**What is accepted in the meantime.** `delete from rules` works. A Rule deleted
that way takes with it the ability to explain every Violation already logged
against it, and nothing warns anyone at the time.

**What the constraints do cover is tested.** A Field that does not belong to its
content, a Flanking value that is not `whitespace`, a Symbol that is more than
one character, an empty reason, a duplicate Rule name on one Field, an Exception
pointing at no Rule — every one of those is refused by the schema as shipped, and
pg-mem enforces all of them. One character is written `looks_for like '_'` rather
than with a length function: it counts characters rather than bytes, which is the
same reading the server makes, and pg-mem has no length function to call.

**Exceptions are rows too, and follow the same discipline.** An Exception belongs
to exactly one Rule, as it always has. Removing one makes its Rule fire where it
previously did not, which is a change to what the Rules do, so an Exception is
disabled rather than deleted for the same reason a Rule is.

**The operator no longer writes YAML.** Rule Sets were YAML held in a text
column, written inside a SQL string with its apostrophes doubled. They are now
ordinary columns. What goes with the YAML is its parser at startup, its parse
error reporting, and the nesting that bound a Rule to a Field — the binding is
now two columns.

**Some checking moves into the database.** A Field that does not belong to the
content, a Flanking value that is not `whitespace`, a Symbol that is not one
character, an empty reason: these were startup refusals and become constraints,
so they are refused when the operator writes them rather than when the server
next starts. That is the better moment — the operator is present. Startup still
refuses a Rule Set it cannot bind, because a constraint cannot express everything
and a database restored from elsewhere is not something the schema witnessed.

**Nothing in `src/` reads this yet.** This ADR and the schema record the design.
The server still reads `rule_sets` and parses YAML, so applying the new schema
alone leaves a server that starts against the old table. Wiring it up is separate
work, and until it is done the two coexist.

> Done in #26. The server reads `rules` and `rule_exceptions`, `rule_sets` is
> gone from the schema, and the YAML parser and its dependency went with it.

**`CONTEXT.md` needs its Rule Set Version entry rewritten.** It currently says
the version is derived from the rule sets as supplied and names the text rather
than the Rules parsed out of it. Both halves are now wrong.

> Done in #21. The entry describes the Rules in force, and #26 adds the rule id
> to what it says the version covers — a Rule renamed is a Rule a caller reads
> differently, so a version that ignored the id would name two Rule Sets as one.
########## 0008-a-default-set-of-rules-ships-as-sql-the-operator-applies.md
# A default set of Rules ships as SQL the operator applies

`default-rules.sql` ships in the repository beside `schema.sql`, and is applied
the same way and by the same hand. It writes 89 checks — 74 Terms and 15
Symbols, for the tells that a piece of writing came from a model — against each
of the five Fields, so 445 Rules arrive, all enabled.

Nothing about the write path changes. The operator applies it, the server reads
what is there at startup, and this project still writes nothing to its own
database (ADR-0006). A Rule is still a row and is still switched off rather than
deleted (ADR-0007), which is how this file is meant to be tuned.

## The ADR-0006 line this sits against

ADR-0006 says the project "ships the schema and stops there: there is no load
command, nothing read off the filesystem, and **no template to copy**." A file of
default Rules is close enough to that last clause to be worth answering rather
than stepping around.

What that clause was rejecting was the loader's templates: files the project read
at runtime, which had to stay in step with the database and gave the project two
representations of the same Rule Sets for the rest of its life. None of that
applies here. Nothing reads `default-rules.sql` at runtime — `grep` finds it in
no source file, no script and no compose service. It is not a second
representation of Rules the database also holds; it is the statements that put
them there once, in the same position `schema.sql` occupies. After it is applied
the database is the only representation, and an operator who tunes a Rule tunes
the row, never the file.

The property ADR-0006 exists to protect is untouched: the generating agent cannot
loosen a Rule that keeps rejecting it (ADR-0001), and neither can anything this
repository ships.

## Considered Options

**A SQL file the operator applies.** Chosen by the maintainer. It costs the
operator one command they are already taking a version of, and the suite runs the
shipped file against an in-process Postgres, so what is documented is what is
tested — the same standard ADR-0006 set for the README's statements.

**The server seeds an empty `rules` table.** Rejected. It is the only option that
is default without the operator doing anything, and it is bought by giving the
server a write path into its own Rules, which reverses ADR-0006 and weakens
ADR-0001 to no purpose. The convenience is one command.

**The tables as README documentation only.** Rejected. Cheapest, and it drifts:
nothing runs it, so nothing catches a Rule that the schema would refuse. Six of
the eighty-nine carry an apostrophe and one is a character that must be a single
code point; none of that survives being retyped out of a table by hand.

**Every Rule shipped disabled.** Considered seriously, and rejected by the
maintainer. It answers the trimming problem directly — nobody decides up front
whether `ensure that` is too noisy, and the operator switches on what earns its
place. It was rejected because a file that does nothing when applied is a file
whose effect is never seen, and because the honest way to learn which Rules are
too noisy is to have them reject something.

## Consequences

**Applying it will reject Test Cases a tester wrote by hand.** This is the known
cost of shipping enabled and untrimmed. `ensure that`, `correctly`, `properly`
and `various` are ordinary QA English, and the QA-specific block is named in the
file as the rows to switch off first. The file is a starting point to tune down,
not a setting to accept.

**The Rules are not this project's opinions.** Every row traces to one of six
published anti-AI-writing references, named in the file's header and read in
`docs/sessions/2026-08-14-anti-ai-writing-rule-tables.md`. Where the references
disagree with the row, the file says so: `no-spaced-semicolon` and
`no-spaced-colon` are recorded in it as catching odd spacing and **not** catching
an AI tell, because the 2026 measurements say models use fewer semicolons than
people do, and a Rule firing on one penalises the human habit. They ship because
they cost nothing, and the file refuses to pretend they are more than that.

**Applying it twice is safe, and does not undo tuning.** Each statement carries
`on conflict (content_kind, field, rule_id) do nothing`, so a Rule already there
is left exactly as it is. An operator who has switched Rules off can re-apply the
file without switching them back on — which matters, because a second `psql -f`
silently pulling back the operator's only lever would make that lever untrustable.

**What the two tables cannot reach is written down in the file.** The full
"it is not X, it is Y" frame, the rule of three, any threshold, thin punctuation,
uniform sentence length, Title Case and the bold-header bullet layout are all out

111	way a test case is — a title and a body — each with its own rule set, so a read
112	carries the violations found in what it serves. They are read only: the API
113	lists them and retrieves one, and there is no endpoint that writes one.
114	
115	This settles the question the README carried as open, "what the reference-document
116	endpoints look like", and it fixes one part of the scope ADR-0004 deliberately
117	left open.
118	
119	## Considered Options
120	
121	**Where the documents live.** A directory on the server, pointed at by an
122	environment variable the way rule sets were, was argued for on the grounds that
123	it ships immediately, needs no new infrastructure, and keeps the boundary that
124	matters — the agent has no local files, and the server having them is exactly
125	the trust boundary. Storing them in TestLink as requirement specifications was
126	argued for as keeping one source of truth. Both were rejected by the maintainer
127	in favour of building the ADR-0004 database now and making documents its first
128	tenant: the store was already decided, and a second temporary store would have
129	been a third place content lives.
130	
131	**Whether a read reports violations.** Serving documents straight through,
132	unchecked, was argued for as the smaller change and the one that invents no
133	vocabulary: a rule set was defined as the rules bound to one field of a test
134	case, and a document had no fields. Rejected by the maintainer. ADR-0003's own
135	reasoning applies to documents at least as strongly as to test cases — the read
136	path is where legacy fingerprints propagate into new cases, and a reference
137	document written in the wording the rules exist to catch is the most direct way
138	for that to happen. Documents therefore gained fields so the rules could reach
139	them.
140	
141	**Whether the agent can write a document.** Full CRUD, matching the test case
142	surface, was considered and rejected. A document the agent could write is a
143	document it could author in the style the rules catch and then read back as
144	authority, which is the same reason ADR-0001 gives it no way to reload a rule.
145	
146	**How content reaches the database.** Seeding on first startup was rejected
147	because it makes the server something that writes its own rules, and because
148	"first startup" is a state that is easy to get wrong on a redeploy. Loading
149	entirely out of band was rejected because it would leave no supported path from
150	a written rule set to a running server. A load command the operator runs was
151	chosen.
152	
153	## Consequences
154	
155	**Rule sets gained a level.** A rule set is now written under the content it
156	checks — `testCase:` or `referenceDocument:` — because the two have different
157	fields and a flat namespace would leave `title` belonging to nothing in
158	particular. Existing rule set files must be re-indented under `testCase:`. The
159	loader refuses a rule set naming anything else, so a file that was not migrated
160	fails loudly rather than binding to nothing and never firing.
161	
162	**The server no longer reads a file.** Rule sets are read from the database at
163	startup, which resolves the tension the README flagged against ADR-0001: there
164	is no mounted path any more. Reading once at startup and never reloading is
165	unchanged, and so is rule set version, which is still derived from the rule set
166	text exactly as supplied.
167	
168	**There is one write path, and the server is not on it.** `npm run load` is the
169	only thing in the project that writes to the database. The object the server
170	holds exposes no write at all, so relaxing a rule or authoring a document is not
171	something the running system can do, whatever reaches it over HTTP.
172	
173	**Rule sets are appended, not replaced.** Superseding a rule set does not destroy
174	the one a running server is still judging by, so an operator can read back,
175	compare or recover what was in force before a load. Nothing in the API resolves a
176	version to its row — reading one back is an operator with a database client, not
177	a feature — so this is history kept cheaply, not a lookup the server offers.
178	
179	**A document's shape is taken from its file.** The file name without its
180	extension is the id a caller retrieves it by; the first line is the title,
181	written as a Markdown heading; the rest is the body. Every file in the directory
182	is read as a document — a file that is not one is refused by name rather than
183	skipped, because a document silently left out is one the agent will never know it
184	was meant to have. Names opening with a dot are the exception, being the
185	operating system's rather than the operator's.
186	
187	**One report covers everything an operator supplied.** The load command checks
188	the rule sets and the documents before writing either, and reports their problems
189	together. A rule set problem must not hide a document problem, or the operator
190	loads twice to find both — the same bargain the server makes at startup when it
191	names every invalid rule at once.
192	########## 0006-rule-sets-and-documents-are-written-with-sql.md
193	# Rule Sets and Reference Documents are written with SQL, and the project ships no loader
194	
195	An operator writes Rule Sets and Reference Documents into the database with SQL,
196	using whatever database client they already have. The project ships the schema
197	and stops there: there is no load command, nothing read off the filesystem, and
198	no template to copy. The server reads the database at startup exactly as before.
199	
200	This reverses the "How content reaches the database" section of ADR-0005, which
201	chose a load command the operator runs. Everything else that ADR settled is
202	untouched — documents are still checked content held in the database, still
203	read-only over the API, still composed of a title and a body with their own Rule
204	Sets.
205	
206	## Considered Options
207	
208	**A load command reading files.** What ADR-0005 chose and what this replaces. Its
209	templates and its directory of documents were the thing that made the database
210	concrete while the schema was being designed; the maintainer's framing is that
211	they were a development intermediate whose job ended when the database became
212	real, and that keeping them means the project carries two representations of the
213	same Rule Sets for the rest of its life.
214	
215	**A write surface on the server, kept off the agent's API.** Rejected. It is the
216	most usable answer for an operator without a database client, but it puts a write
217	path on the process ADR-0001 exists to keep off one, and defends the property by
218	network reachability rather than by the server holding an object that cannot
219	write. The weaker guarantee was not worth the convenience.
220	
221	**Writing with SQL, out of band.** Chosen by the maintainer. ADR-0005 rejected
222	this on the grounds that it leaves no supported path from a written Rule Set to a
223	running server. That objection is answered rather than dismissed: the schema
224	ships in the repository as `schema.sql`, the README documents the statements that
225	write a Rule Set and a Reference Document, and the suite extracts and runs those
226	statements against an in-process Postgres, so what is documented is what is
227	tested. The path is supported; it is simply not automated.
228	
229	ADR-0005's other objection, to seeding on first startup, is not answered because
230	it no longer applies: nothing seeds. The server gained no write, and "first
231	startup" is not a state anything here behaves differently in.
232	
233	## Consequences
234	
235	**The project no longer writes to its own database, at all.** ADR-0005 recorded
236	"there is one write path, and the server is not on it". There is now no write
237	path in the project. What ADR-0001 protects is stronger for it, not weaker: the
238	agent cannot relax a Rule that keeps rejecting it, and neither can anything this
239	repository ships.
240	
241	**YAML stays, as the storage format.** Rule Sets are held as text in
242	`rule_sets.source` and parsed at startup, which is what the load command already
243	wrote and what the server already read. Removing the loader does not remove
244	YAML — an operator writes YAML inside a SQL statement — so the Rule Set
245	vocabulary, its checking, and the Rule Set Version derived from the text as
246	supplied are all unchanged.
247	
248	**A Reference Document's shape is no longer taken from a file.** Its id, and its
249	two Fields, were read out of a file name and a Markdown heading; an operator now
250	writes all three directly. The Rules that reach a document are unchanged, and so
251	is what a read reports. What goes is the file convention and the refusal of a
252	file that is not a document.
253	
254	**Applying the schema becomes an operator's step.** The load command created the
255	tables on first use. A fresh database now has none until `schema.sql` is applied,
256	so the server's refusal to start has to name that step rather than a command that
257	no longer exists. A database with no schema is still told apart from a database
258	that is unreachable, exactly as before.
259	
260	**Nothing checks what an operator wrote before the server binds it.** The load
261	command validated Rule Sets and documents together and reported every problem in
262	one pass. Startup still refuses invalid Rule Sets and still reports every problem
263	at once, so that check survives — it happens when the server starts rather than
264	when the Rule Set is written. A malformed Reference Document is no longer refused
265	at all: its Fields are whatever the operator wrote.
266	########## 0007-a-rule-is-a-row-and-is-disabled-rather-than-deleted.md
267	# A Rule is a row, and is disabled rather than deleted
268	
269	Rule Sets stop being one YAML document held as text and become rows, one per
270	Rule. A Rule carries the content and the Field it binds to, which kind of check
271	it is, what it looks for, the reason it gives, and a switch. An operator adds one
272	Rule, or turns one off, with a single statement naming that Rule alone.
273	
274	Nothing is deleted. A Rule that should stop firing is disabled, and its row
275	stays. What a Rule looks for is not edited either — the reason it gives is. Both
276	are a discipline the schema documents and does not enforce, which is a decision
277	rather than an omission: there is one operator, and a guard's value is entirely
278	in who it stops.
279	
280	This changes only how Rule Sets are stored and edited. They are still read once
281	at startup and never reloaded (ADR-0004), still written by an operator with SQL
282	with nothing in the project writing (ADR-0006), and a Rule still binds to exactly
283	one Field of one kind of content.
284	
285	## Considered Options
286	
287	**One YAML document, appended.** What this replaces. Its virtue is that the Rule
288	Set Version falls straight out of the bytes, and that a superseded document stays
289	readable because a new one is inserted beside it rather than over it. Its cost is
290	that every edit is an edit to the whole thing: turning off one Rule means
291	retyping every other Rule into a fresh `insert`, and a Rule Set of sixty Rules is
292	a wall of text where a one-character slip in an unrelated Rule is invisible. The
293	maintainer's framing is that a Rule Set is a list of independent checks and
294	should be edited as one.
295	
296	**Rows, deleted when no longer wanted.** The obvious shape, and rejected. Every
297	response names the Rule Set Version and every Violation is logged against it, so
298	the system has already promised to explain a rejection after the fact. A deleted
299	Rule breaks that promise silently: the log still names the Rule, and the Rule is
300	not there to be read. The test cases rejected by it stay rejected and become
301	unexplainable, which lands on the QA engineer who wrote them rather than on the
302	operator who deleted the Rule. Delete also buys very little — a disabled Rule
303	stops firing exactly as completely as a deleted one, so what is saved is table
304	size, at a scale (tens of rows) no database notices.
305	
306	**Rows, disabled rather than deleted.** Chosen. `enabled` is both the switch and
307	the tombstone, so the operator has three operations rather than four and the
308	record of what once fired survives. Turning a Rule back on is one statement and
309	restores the exact Rule that was there, rather than a retyped approximation of
310	it.
311	
312	**A table per kind — one for Terms, one for Symbols.** Considered because the
313	columns differ: a Symbol carries Flanking and a Term does not. Rejected. A
314	Field's Rule Set is one list that mixes both, so two tables means every read is a
315	union and every operation an operator performs has to start by working out which
316	table the Rule is in. One table with a column naming the kind keeps the statement
317	shapes identical.
318	
319	## Consequences
320	
321	**The Rule Set Version is derived from the Rules in force, not from text.** It
322	was a hash of the YAML exactly as supplied; there is no longer a document to
323	hash. It becomes a hash over the enabled Rules, rendered in a fixed order and
324	including everything a caller was judged by — the Field, the kind, what is looked
325	for, the Flanking, the reason, and the Exceptions. Disabled Rules are left out,
326	because they judge nothing.
327	
328	What the version is for is unchanged: it names the Rules a response was produced
329	by, and it cannot go on naming Rules that have since been edited. One property
330	improves. Because the version comes from the Rules rather than from their
331	formatting, the same Rules always produce the same version — so a Rule disabled
332	and later enabled again returns the Rule Set to the version it had before, rather
333	than to a new one that means the same thing. Under the old scheme, reformatting
334	the YAML changed the version without changing a Rule; that no longer happens, and
335	the safety argument for it no longer applies, because there is no formatting left
336	to change.
337	
338	**What a Rule looks for cannot be edited; what it says can.** Changing `looks_for`
339	or the kind of check makes it a different check under the same name, and every
340	Violation already logged against that name then describes something that never
341	happened. Changing the reason changes only the wording the caller is handed.
342	Rewording a reason changes the Rule Set Version, which is correct: what a caller
343	is told is part of what the Rules do.
344	
345	An operator who wants a Rule to look for something else disables it and adds
346	another, which is the honest shape of that change anyway.
347	
348	**The discipline is not enforced, and that is decided rather than left open.**
349	Everywhere else, this project has made the unwanted thing impossible rather than
350	forbidden — the server holds an object with no write (ADR-0006), the agent has no
351	reload endpoint (ADR-0004). This is the exception, and it is worth naming as one.
352	
353	The enforcing move exists: a trigger refusing a `delete` on `rules`, and refusing
354	an update that touches the identity columns, naming what to do instead. Postgres
355	takes it. What it cannot do is live in `schema.sql`, because the suite runs the
356	shipped schema against pg-mem, and pg-mem cannot parse
357	`create function ... language plpgsql` — adding the trigger makes the schema
358	unrunnable there and fails thirteen tests. So enforcing it means either giving
359	the suite a real Postgres, or shipping the trigger in a second file the suite
360	does not run.
361	
362	**Chosen by the maintainer: neither. The discipline stays a discipline**, written
363	in the schema's comments and in this ADR, with nothing stopping a `delete`.
364	
365	The reason is the whole of it: **there is one operator, and it is the maintainer.**
366	A guard's value is entirely in who it stops. It stops the person who does not know
367	the rule, or who has forgotten it — and here there is no such person. Paying for a
368	wall against yourself, today, is paying for nothing. The other two options were
369	priced at roughly thirty-five lines and one afternoon, and at a test suite that
370	must start a real database; neither is expensive, and both buy the same nothing
371	while the operator count is one.
372	
373	An API in front of the database was raised and rejected on the merits, twice over.
374	It would give this project the write path ADR-0001 and ADR-0006 exist to remove,
375	and it would not even work: the operator writes SQL directly, so they are already
376	past any door an API could guard.
377	
378	**What makes this reversible, and what the trigger would be.** The day a second
379	person writes SQL against this database, the calculation changes and this should
380	be revisited. The upgrade is small and does not disturb anything here: a
381	`schema-guards.sql` carrying the trigger, applied once, plus a startup check
382	asking whether the guard is installed and refusing to start when it is not. That
383	check is a read, so the server gains no write and ADR-0006 is untouched. It is
384	recorded here so the option does not have to be rediscovered.
385	
386	**What is accepted in the meantime.** `delete from rules` works. A Rule deleted
387	that way takes with it the ability to explain every Violation already logged
388	against it, and nothing warns anyone at the time.
389	
390	**What the constraints do cover is tested.** A Field that does not belong to its
391	content, a Flanking value that is not `whitespace`, a Symbol that is more than
392	one character, an empty reason, a duplicate Rule name on one Field, an Exception
393	pointing at no Rule — every one of those is refused by the schema as shipped, and
394	pg-mem enforces all of them. One character is written `looks_for like '_'` rather
395	than with a length function: it counts characters rather than bytes, which is the
396	same reading the server makes, and pg-mem has no length function to call.
397	
398	**Exceptions are rows too, and follow the same discipline.** An Exception belongs
399	to exactly one Rule, as it always has. Removing one makes its Rule fire where it
400	previously did not, which is a change to what the Rules do, so an Exception is
401	disabled rather than deleted for the same reason a Rule is.
402	
403	**The operator no longer writes YAML.** Rule Sets were YAML held in a text
404	column, written inside a SQL string with its apostrophes doubled. They are now
405	ordinary columns. What goes with the YAML is its parser at startup, its parse
406	error reporting, and the nesting that bound a Rule to a Field — the binding is
407	now two columns.
408	
409	**Some checking moves into the database.** A Field that does not belong to the
410	content, a Flanking value that is not `whitespace`, a Symbol that is not one
411	character, an empty reason: these were startup refusals and become constraints,
412	so they are refused when the operator writes them rather than when the server
413	next starts. That is the better moment — the operator is present. Startup still
414	refuses a Rule Set it cannot bind, because a constraint cannot express everything
415	and a database restored from elsewhere is not something the schema witnessed.
416	
417	**Nothing in `src/` reads this yet.** This ADR and the schema record the design.
418	The server still reads `rule_sets` and parses YAML, so applying the new schema
419	alone leaves a server that starts against the old table. Wiring it up is separate
420	work, and until it is done the two coexist.
421	
422	> Done in #26. The server reads `rules` and `rule_exceptions`, `rule_sets` is
423	> gone from the schema, and the YAML parser and its dependency went with it.
424	
425	**`CONTEXT.md` needs its Rule Set Version entry rewritten.** It currently says
426	the version is derived from the rule sets as supplied and names the text rather
427	than the Rules parsed out of it. Both halves are now wrong.
428	
429	> Done in #21. The entry describes the Rules in force, and #26 adds the rule id
430	> to what it says the version covers — a Rule renamed is a Rule a caller reads
431	> differently, so a version that ignored the id would name two Rule Sets as one.
432	########## 0008-a-default-set-of-rules-ships-as-sql-the-operator-applies.md
433	# A default set of Rules ships as SQL the operator applies
434	
435	`default-rules.sql` ships in the repository beside `schema.sql`, and is applied
436	the same way and by the same hand. It writes 89 checks — 74 Terms and 15
437	Symbols, for the tells that a piece of writing came from a model — against each
438	of the five Fields, so 445 Rules arrive, all enabled.
439	
440	Nothing about the write path changes. The operator applies it, the server reads
441	what is there at startup, and this project still writes nothing to its own
442	database (ADR-0006). A Rule is still a row and is still switched off rather than
443	deleted (ADR-0007), which is how this file is meant to be tuned.
444	
445	## The ADR-0006 line this sits against
446	
447	ADR-0006 says the project "ships the schema and stops there: there is no load
448	command, nothing read off the filesystem, and **no template to copy**." A file of
449	default Rules is close enough to that last clause to be worth answering rather
450	than stepping around.
451	
452	What that clause was rejecting was the loader's templates: files the project read
453	at runtime, which had to stay in step with the database and gave the project two
454	representations of the same Rule Sets for the rest of its life. None of that
455	applies here. Nothing reads `default-rules.sql` at runtime — `grep` finds it in
456	no source file, no script and no compose service. It is not a second
457	representation of Rules the database also holds; it is the statements that put
458	them there once, in the same position `schema.sql` occupies. After it is applied
459	the database is the only representation, and an operator who tunes a Rule tunes
460	the row, never the file.
461	
462	The property ADR-0006 exists to protect is untouched: the generating agent cannot
463	loosen a Rule that keeps rejecting it (ADR-0001), and neither can anything this
464	repository ships.
465	
466	## Considered Options
467	
468	**A SQL file the operator applies.** Chosen by the maintainer. It costs the
469	operator one command they are already taking a version of, and the suite runs the
470	shipped file against an in-process Postgres, so what is documented is what is
471	tested — the same standard ADR-0006 set for the README's statements.
472	
473	**The server seeds an empty `rules` table.** Rejected. It is the only option that
474	is default without the operator doing anything, and it is bought by giving the
475	server a write path into its own Rules, which reverses ADR-0006 and weakens
476	ADR-0001 to no purpose. The convenience is one command.
477	
478	**The tables as README documentation only.** Rejected. Cheapest, and it drifts:
479	nothing runs it, so nothing catches a Rule that the schema would refuse. Six of
480	the eighty-nine carry an apostrophe and one is a character that must be a single
481	code point; none of that survives being retyped out of a table by hand.
482	
483	**Every Rule shipped disabled.** Considered seriously, and rejected by the
484	maintainer. It answers the trimming problem directly — nobody decides up front
485	whether `ensure that` is too noisy, and the operator switches on what earns its
486	place. It was rejected because a file that does nothing when applied is a file
487	whose effect is never seen, and because the honest way to learn which Rules are
488	too noisy is to have them reject something.
489	
490	## Consequences
491	
492	**Applying it will reject Test Cases a tester wrote by hand.** This is the known
493	cost of shipping enabled and untrimmed. `ensure that`, `correctly`, `properly`
494	and `various` are ordinary QA English, and the QA-specific block is named in the
495	file as the rows to switch off first. The file is a starting point to tune down,
496	not a setting to accept.
497	
498	**The Rules are not this project's opinions.** Every row traces to one of six
499	published anti-AI-writing references, named in the file's header and read in
500	`docs/sessions/2026-08-14-anti-ai-writing-rule-tables.md`. Where the references
501	disagree with the row, the file says so: `no-spaced-semicolon` and
502	`no-spaced-colon` are recorded in it as catching odd spacing and **not** catching
503	an AI tell, because the 2026 measurements say models use fewer semicolons than
504	people do, and a Rule firing on one penalises the human habit. They ship because
505	they cost nothing, and the file refuses to pretend they are more than that.
506	
507	**Applying it twice is safe, and does not undo tuning.** Each statement carries
508	`on conflict (content_kind, field, rule_id) do nothing`, so a Rule already there
509	is left exactly as it is. An operator who has switched Rules off can re-apply the
510	file without switching them back on — which matters, because a second `psql -f`
511	silently pulling back the operator's only lever would make that lever untrustable.
512	
513	**What the two tables cannot reach is written down in the file.** The full
514	"it is not X, it is Y" frame, the rule of three, any threshold, thin punctuation,
515	uniform sentence length, Title Case and the bold-header bullet layout are all out
516	of reach of a Term and a Symbol. They are listed in the file so an absent Rule is
517	not read as a clean area. Closing the first of them needs a third kind of check,
518	with holes in it, and nothing here is blocked on that.
519	
520	**A Term is literal, so an apostrophe is two Rules' worth of coverage.** The six
521	Terms carrying one hold a straight apostrophe, and the same phrase written with a
522	curly one does not match them. It is still caught, by `no-curly-apostrophe` firing
523	on the character, but under that Rule and with that reason.
